paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.mainContribution: Proposes the Transformer, a sequence transduction model built entirely from multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers, with no recurrence or convolution. It is more parallelizable and faster to train, and reaches new state-of-the-art BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French translation, and generalizes to English constituency parsing.
paper.abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

firstPage.introduction: Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states \(h_{t}\), as a function of the previous hidden state \(h_{t-1}\) and the input for position \(t\). This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduction models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

overview.plain: This paper introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction model that turns one sequence of words into another using only attention, with no step-by-step recurrence or convolution. Because its work can run in parallel, it trains faster, and it reaches top translation scores for English to German and English to French, and it also works on parsing English sentences.

story.text: Older language systems read a sentence one word at a time, so each step waits for the one before it.
story.technical: Here the paper uses recurrent neural networks, which compute hidden states \(h_{t}\) from the previous state \(h_{t-1}\) and the input at position \(t\), to show why sequential computation blocks parallel training.

story.text: Attention, which lets a word look at any other word directly, was already used but was attached to these step-by-step networks.
story.technical: Here the paper uses the attention mechanism, a weighted sum over values scored by compatibility with a query, as the only source of dependencies between positions, removing recurrence and convolution from the encoder-decoder design.

story.text: The Transformer keeps an input side that reads the sentence and an output side that writes the translation, with words first turned into vectors and given position information.
story.technical: Here the paper uses an encoder that maps the input sequence \((x_{1},...,x_{n})\) to representations \(\mathbf{z}\), learned word embeddings that turn tokens into vectors, and sine and cosine positional encodings added to them so the model knows word order.

story.text: The core operation compares each position's query with every key, turns those matches into weights, and averages the values using those weights.
story.technical: Here the paper uses scaled dot-product attention, \(\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}})V\), where dot products of queries \(Q\) with keys \(K\) are divided by \(\sqrt{d_{k}}\) and converted by softmax into weights on the values \(V\).

story.text: Several attention heads run side by side, each looking at the words through its own learned view, and their results are combined.
story.technical: Here the paper uses multi-head attention, which runs \(h=8\) attention heads on projected queries, keys and values with \(d_{k}=d_{v}=d_{\text{model}}/h=64\), then concatenates the outputs and projects them with \(W^{O}\).

story.text: When the translation is written one word at a time, the decoder is blocked from looking ahead at words not yet produced, and each new word is fed back in as input.
story.technical: Here the paper uses masked self-attention in the decoder so that the predictions for position \(i\) depend only on outputs at positions less than \(i\), with auto-regressive generation consuming previously generated symbols as input.

story.text: Each layer adds its input back to its output and normalizes the result, and it includes a small two-step feed-forward network applied to each position.
story.technical: Here the paper uses residual connections with layer normalization, so each sub-layer output is \(\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x+\mathrm{Sublayer}(x))\), and a position-wise feed-forward network made of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation between them.

story.text: On English-to-German and English-to-French translation, BLEU, a score that measures how closely a machine translation matches human reference translations, reached new top results, and the same model also worked on English parsing.
story.technical: Here the paper uses BLEU scores on WMT 2014 translation tasks, with the Adam optimizer and a warmup learning-rate schedule during training, to report that the Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German and 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French.

branches.name: Linear algebra and neural network basics
branches.description: The vector, matrix, normalization and layer primitives that every later component is built from.

concepts.name: Vectors and matrices
concepts.whyNeeded: Queries, keys, values, embeddings and weight matrices are all vectors or matrices multiplied together throughout the model.
concepts.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.
concepts.plainRole: Queries, keys, values and weights are all vectors or matrices multiplied together to produce the model's outputs.

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.whyNeeded: Attention scores are computed as dot products between queries and keys, and the paper motivates scaling by examining their magnitude.
concepts.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys
concepts.plainRole: Dot products measure how well each query matches each key, producing the attention scores.

concepts.name: Softmax function
concepts.whyNeeded: Softmax turns attention scores into weights that sum to one, and also converts decoder outputs into next-token probabilities.
concepts.quote: We also use the usual learned linear transformation and softmax function to convert the decoder output to predicted next-token probabilities.
concepts.plainRole: Softmax turns attention scores into weights that add up to one, and also turns decoder outputs into next-word probabilities.

concepts.name: Feed-forward neural network layer
concepts.whyNeeded: Each layer contains a position-wise feed-forward sub-network made of two linear maps with a ReLU between them.
concepts.quote: This consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between.
concepts.plainRole: Each layer includes a feed-forward sub-network applied separately to each position, built from two linear maps with a ReLU between them.

branches.name: Sequence modeling background
branches.description: The recurrent and encoder-decoder setup the paper argues against, plus the token and generation machinery it still uses.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural networks
concepts.whyNeeded: The paper defines its contribution against RNNs, whose step-by-step hidden-state computation the Transformer removes.
concepts.quote: Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences.
concepts.plainRole: The paper defines its contribution against recurrent networks, which process symbols in order and cannot be parallelized within an example.

concepts.name: Word embeddings
concepts.whyNeeded: Input and output tokens are first converted into learned dense vectors before any attention is applied.
concepts.quote: we use learned embeddings to convert the input tokens and output tokens to vectors
concepts.plainRole: Input and output tokens are converted into learned vectors before any attention is applied.

concepts.name: Encoder-decoder architecture
concepts.whyNeeded: The Transformer keeps the encoder-decoder layout, mapping an input sequence to representations and generating the output from them.
concepts.quote: The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder
concepts.plainRole: The Transformer keeps the encoder-decoder layout: the encoder reads the input and the decoder produces the output from it.

concepts.name: Tokenization
concepts.whyNeeded: Sentences are split into subword units such as byte-pair or word-piece tokens before they become model inputs and vocabulary entries.
concepts.quote: Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.
concepts.plainRole: Input text is split into tokens, and training batches are formed from roughly equal numbers of source and target tokens.

concepts.name: Auto-regressive generation
concepts.whyNeeded: The decoder produces one symbol at a time, feeding earlier outputs back as input, which determines how translations are produced and scored.
concepts.quote: consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.
concepts.plainRole: The decoder produces one symbol at a time, feeding earlier outputs back as input, which shapes how translations are produced and scored.

branches.name: Attention machinery
branches.description: The attention computation, its multi-head and masked variants, and the position signal that makes attention order-aware.

concepts.name: Positional encoding
concepts.whyNeeded: Because there is no recurrence or convolution, sine and cosine position signals must be added to embeddings so the model knows token order.
concepts.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence
concepts.plainRole: With no recurrence or convolution, position signals must be added to embeddings so the model can use the order of the sequence.

concepts.name: Attention mechanism
concepts.whyNeeded: The whole model relies on attention to draw dependencies between positions, so the reader must know how a weighted sum over values is formed from query-key compatibility.
concepts.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function
concepts.plainRole: Attention is the mechanism the whole model uses to connect positions, forming weighted sums of values based on query-key compatibility.

concepts.name: Scaled dot-product attention
concepts.whyNeeded: This is the exact attention operation used everywhere in the model, including the softmax of scaled query-key products applied to values.
concepts.quote: We suspect that for large values of \(d_{k}\), the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients.
concepts.quoteDisplay: We suspect that for large values of \(d_{k}\), the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients.
concepts.plainRole: This is the exact attention operation used throughout the model, with scaling to keep softmax gradients from becoming very small.

concepts.name: Multi-head attention
concepts.whyNeeded: The model runs h parallel attention heads on projected inputs, and the central claim of its encoder and decoder depends on this design.
concepts.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.
concepts.plainRole: Several attention heads run in parallel so the model can jointly attend to different representation subspaces and positions.

concepts.name: Masked self-attention in the decoder
concepts.whyNeeded: The decoder masks illegal future positions so that generation stays auto-regressive during training.
concepts.quote: We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property.
concepts.section: 3.2.3 Applications of Attention in our Model
concepts.plainRole: Masking blocks the decoder from seeing future positions, preserving the auto-regressive property during training.

branches.name: Transformer block and stack
branches.description: How attention and feed-forward sub-layers are combined with residual connections and normalization into the full model.

concepts.name: Residual connections and layer normalization
concepts.whyNeeded: Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), so the layer equation cannot be followed without it.
concepts.quote: Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization.
concepts.plainRole: Each sub-layer is wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization, which the layer equation relies on.

concepts.name: Transformer architecture
concepts.whyNeeded: This is the main object of the paper: a stack of encoder and decoder layers built only from attention, feed-forward, normalization and positional components.
concepts.quote: In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.
concepts.plainRole: This is the paper's main object: a stack of encoder and decoder layers built only from attention, feed-forward, normalization and position components.

branches.name: Training and evaluation
branches.description: The optimizer used to train the model and the BLEU metric used to score its translations.

concepts.name: BLEU score
concepts.whyNeeded: The headline results are reported as BLEU scores on WMT 2014 translation tasks, so the reader must know what the number measures.
concepts.quote: Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.
concepts.plainRole: BLEU is the score used to report the headline translation results, so readers need it to judge the claimed improvements.

concepts.name: Adam optimizer with warmup learning-rate schedule
concepts.whyNeeded: Models are trained with Adam and a learning rate that rises during warmup and then decays with the inverse square root of the step number.
concepts.quote: We varied the learning rate over the course of training
concepts.plainRole: Models are trained with Adam while the learning rate is varied over training, following a warmup schedule.

bleu-score.description: A metric scoring machine translation output by n-gram overlap with reference translations.

softmax-function.description: Turning a vector of scores into a probability distribution.

resource.why: A simple explanation of what softmax does to arbitrary scores and how to implement it, which is exactly what a beginner needs.

feed-forward-neural-networks.name: Feed-forward neural networks
feed-forward-neural-networks.description: Layers of weighted sums and nonlinear activations.

resource.title: Feed-Forward Neural Networks Explained: A Complete Tutorial
resource.why: A complete beginner-level explainer covering layers, weighted sums, and nonlinear activations in a feed-forward network.

recurrent-neural-networks.name: Recurrent neural networks
recurrent-neural-networks.description: Networks that process sequences step by step (RNN, LSTM, GRU).

resource.why: A beginner-friendly walkthrough that explains how RNNs process sequences step by step and shows a from-scratch implementation.

resource.why: Walks through training word embeddings from scratch in a simple Keras sentiment model and then visualizing them, so a beginner sees what a dense token vector is and how it gets learned.

encoder-decoder-architecture.name: Encoder-decoder architecture
encoder-decoder-architecture.description: A model that maps an input sequence to hidden representations with an encoder, then generates an output sequence with a decoder.

resource.why: Jay Alammar's illustrated walkthrough shows step by step how an encoder compresses an input sentence and a decoder generates the output, which is ideal for a visual first introduction.

positional-encoding.name: Positional encoding
positional-encoding.description: Vectors added to token embeddings that encode each token's position in a sequence, often with sine and cosine functions.

resource.title: Transformer Architecture: The Positional Encoding - Amirhossein Kazemnejad's Blog
resource.why: A long, step-by-step explainer that motivates why positions must be injected and derives the sinusoidal encoding, which suits a beginner well.

layer-normalization-and-residual-connect.name: Layer normalization and residual connections
layer-normalization-and-residual-connect.description: Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), so the layer equation depends on both pieces.

tokenization.name: Tokenization
tokenization.description: Splitting text into subword units such as byte-pair encoding.

resource.title: Tokenization algorithms
resource.why: Explains byte pair encoding, WordPiece, and Unigram side by side, directly covering the subword splitting the topic describes.

attention-mechanism.name: Attention mechanism
attention-mechanism.description: Weighting inputs by learned relevance (queries, keys, values).

resource.title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep ... | 3Blue1Brown
resource.why: Visual, step-by-step lesson on queries, keys, and values that gives beginners strong intuition for how attention weights inputs.

auto-regressive-generation.name: Auto-regressive generation
auto-regressive-generation.description: The decoder produces one symbol at a time conditioned on earlier outputs, and the masking design depends on this property.

resource.title: How does autoregressive text generation work at inference time?
resource.why: A short FAQ that explains the token-by-token loop where each generated token is appended to the input and the process repeats.

scaled-dot-product-attention.name: Scaled dot-product attention
scaled-dot-product-attention.description: Attention that computes softmax of query-key dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension, then weights the values.

resource.title: Transformer, Part 3: Attention: Queries, Keys and Values · Ishwar Jangid
resource.why: Walks through queries, keys and values and explains clearly why scores are divided by the square root of the key size.

multi-head-attention.name: Multi-head attention
multi-head-attention.description: The model runs several attention heads in parallel over projected queries, keys and values, which is central to the architecture.

resource.title: Multi-Head Attention (MHA) | Sebastian Raschka, PhD
resource.why: A concise, beginner-oriented description of multi-head attention and how each token attends to earlier tokens across several heads.

masked-self-attention-in-the-decoder.name: Masked self-attention in the decoder
masked-self-attention-in-the-decoder.description: Masking illegal connections preserves the auto-regressive property, so the decoder cannot see future outputs during training.

resource.title: Masked self-attention: How LLMs learn relationships between tokens - Stack Overflow
resource.why: A plain-language explanation of how masking blocks future tokens and why this matters for next-token prediction.

resource.title: The Illustrated Transformer – Jay Alammar – Visualizing machine learning one concept at a time.
resource.why: Jay Alammar's visual walkthrough explains self-attention, encoder and decoder stacks, and positional encoding step by step, which suits a complete beginner.

resource.title: Adam Optimizer Tutorial: Intuition and Implementation in Python
resource.why: Explains the intuition behind Adam with an accessible analogy before moving to implementation, making the adaptive per-parameter step sizes easy to grasp.
